name: Urine and goat milk tooth whitening

image.caption: Urine and goat milk tooth whitening

lead: Urine and goat milk whitening is a historical practice in which Roman-era dentists are reported to have cleaned and brightened teeth with a mixture of urine and goat milk. White teeth were associated with beauty and wealth, so the practice sits in the long history of people trying to make their smiles look brighter.
The approach is known mainly from historical accounts of tooth whitening. No clinical trials of it exist, and modern whitening relies on peroxide-based products and professional treatment.

paras: Historical accounts describe the mixture as a rinse or rub applied to the teeth. It is not a current dental product, and modern whitening options are offered as strips, trays, toothpastes and in-office treatments.

Urine is a bodily waste fluid, and the Wikipedia article on urine therapy states that no scientific evidence supports health claims for urine use. Dental organizations describe modern peroxide whitening as the studied route, with sensitivity as its commonest side effect.

angle.text: Historically, the mixture was used to make teeth look whiter, reflecting the long-standing link between bright teeth and attractiveness. It is a historical curiosity in appearance culture rather than a current product.

lead: Urine and goat milk tooth whitening is a historical cosmetic practice in which ancient Roman dentists are reported to have used urine mixed with goat milk to whiten teeth.[1] It belongs to a long tradition of brightening the teeth for appearance, since pearly white teeth have symbolised beauty and wealth.[1]

Urine as a tooth-cleaning ingredient is noted separately in the Wikipedia entry on urine therapy, which says Roman dentists used it for whitening and cites a 2010 book.[2] Urine contains urea and other solutes, and ammonia-like compounds from urine breakdown have been cited in discussions of why it was thought to clean.[2]
No clinical study has tested the mixture. Modern tooth whitening centres on carbamide and hydrogen peroxide products, with tooth sensitivity the most commonly reported effect.[1]

paras: Reports of the practice come from histories of tooth whitening, which describe Roman dentists using urine mixed with goat milk.[1] The surrounding culture linked white teeth with beauty and wealth.[1]

Other historical whitening approaches included oil pulling in Ayurvedic medicine, honey, burnt salt and vinegar recommended by the medieval surgeon Guy de Chauliac, and later barbers who filed teeth and applied acid, which whitened them while eroding enamel.[1] Elsewhere, Japan practised the opposite aesthetic, ohaguro, blackening teeth with an iron-and-tannin dye.[3]
Urine therapy more broadly was popularised in the early 20th century by John W. Armstrong, whose 1944 book The Water of Life became a founding text of the field.[2]

No studies found. Studies of modern peroxide whitening report tooth sensitivity in a majority of people receiving in-office treatment, and the urine therapy article states that no scientific evidence supports health claims for urine therapy.[2][1]

Modern sources note that acidic or abrasive whitening methods can wear enamel.[1] Urine therapy sources describe urine as over 95 percent water with urea, chloride, sodium, potassium and creatinine as main solutes.[2]

timeline.event: Dentists reported to whiten teeth with urine and goat milk.[1]
Armstrong publishes The Water of Life, popularising urine therapy.[2]
